articles.text: 2nd reading of proposed lease extension of PCA The Piedmont City Council will review and consider an application on behalf of Gulf South Towers (GST) to construct a 95-foot-tall telecommunications tower in the city’s Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue. The review will take place on April 19, following Planning Commission approval on March 8. The tower would improve wireless cell phone coverage in Moraga Canyon and its surrounding neighborhoods. GST has applied to use a portion of the city’s Corporation Yard, where a 30-foot wireless pole already exists. The existing installation is not capable of accommodating new technology equipment, such as 5G, and it is not capable of providing service for multiple carriers. Currently, the tower is servicing T-Mobile. City Planner Kevin Jackson noted that city staff had recognized the current facility’s lease had expired and that it was underserving the area. “We looked for a provider who might build a tower that would co-locate with other carriers, because that’s something that the [city code] requires,” he said. “Co-locating with other carriers will also eliminate the number of cell towers needed in the city,” he added. During its March 8 Planning Commission meeting, residents of Moraga Canyon and its surrounding neighborhoods questioned whether the tower would have impacts on property value, and views. Piedmont Center for the Arts Also on the April 19 City Council agenda is the second reading of a proposed extension of the city’s current 10-year lease with the non-profit Piedmont Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue. Council approved terms of the lease extension at a first reading on November 16. Since that time, city staff has recommended some major changes, including rent payment, reducing the time of occupancy by the Center, an early termination clause, and prior written consent for non-arts related rentals.

articles.text: A look at evolution of California Electrical Grid I got interested in studying the California electric grid as the result of the passage of Measure UU for the new aquatic facility. The amount of energy consumed by an aquatic facility is not trivial. Based on the 2019 utility bills the existing 3 pools used 25,396 therms of gas and 110 MWh of electricity a year, equivalent to 854 MWh. The new aquatic facility is planned to have three times the surface and therefore could need three times more energy in a steady state. Clearly the new facility ought to minimize greenhouse gases (GHG) emissions. Given the expected lifetime of the future facility, it makes sense to look forward and consider its GHG footprint in the long term in the context of the evolution of the grid, the City Climate Action Plan and the State 2050 decarbonisation goals. I built a simulation engine for the California grid based on the hourly empirical data available for the year 2019 from the Energy Information Agency (EIA) and the California Public Utility Commission. It simulates the way the energy available from various in-state and outof-state sources are fed into the grid to meet demand. Increase in wind and solar supply is assumed to be based on scaling existing farms, therefore resulting in a proportional increase in such hourly energy offered to the grid. Demand is scaled based on the projection of the adoption of electric vehicles, the construction of new all-electric homes, and the conversion to electricity of residential, commercial, and industrial natural gas usage. Each sector has its own specific hourly demand distribution. Wind and solar are energy sources with very large up and down swings. The graph is the result of running scenarios on the simulator corresponding to the projected demand in 2045. Full grid decarbonization by only using renewable energies: non-fossil dispatchable and wind & solar 2045 demand of 368 TWh, a 45% increase over 2019. It consists of 2019 demand plus 9.7 million all-electric vehicles, plus 2.08 million new all-electric home, plus 66% of all residential and commercial natural gas end users converted to electricity, each demand with its own hourly distribution. Hourly dispatchable energy floor same as 2019: 8,656 MWh. I would favor a single smaller pool focused on sports rather than recreation because of my belief that frugality is essential to meet the climate challenge. In any case, I know that a competent team focused on sustainability is working on the design of a “green” pool and I am confident that the promises of Measure UU will be achieved to the satisfaction of our community. articles.text: Something in our nature inspires humans to collect religious trinkets—talismans and relics that remind us of life’s transcendent mysteries, or icons through which we glimpse the divine. I’ve got dozens of such pious knickknacks – everything from a small collection of large Bibles to a cross necklace – but I suspect the most important of my faith-based souvenirs is a plastic dashboard Jesus figurine that sits up on the back of my stove beside an empty bottle of Calvin beer from Geneva, my daughter’s Albert Einstein action figure and a miniature Moses, which bends like Gumby. My dashboard Jesus is like just about any other dashboard Jesus: the Son of Man sits on a spring with a goofy molded smile and his hands lifted up as if to invoke some kind of blessing. This is Jesus Junk writ large. I should be quick to point out that the importance of my dashboard Jesus lies not in its sentimental value or in its intrinsic worth. They hardly broke the mold when they made this version of the Jeez; one just like mine can be had for less than $10 on eBay. I won’t shed any tears if the little guy catches fire while I’m flambéing mushroom sauce, but I will replace my dashboard Jesus should any ill befall him, because he represents an important spiritual truth: those of us who take our religion seriously should never lose the ability to laugh at our piety. This is not to say that we should mock God or ridicule what is sacred; rather, it is ourselves and our zealous posturing that needs an occasional palliative guffaw. When people lose a sense of humor, they are inspired by faith to engage in all sorts of heinous tomfoolery. I think of Christians who oppose marriage equality on the faulty assumption that one person’s beliefs can dictate another person’s love life; or I think of people killing one another in the name of God in places like Gaza, Syria, Myanmar, and heaven-knows-where else. articles.text: Alameda County opened COVID-19 vaccination appointments to all adult residents age 16 and older on Monday, April 12. Vaccines manufactured by Moderna are approved for people ages 18 and older. Pfizer vaccines are currently approved for teenagers as young as 16. Alameda County has a form to receive notifications about available appointments at covid-19. acgov.org/vaccines Californians are also encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, employer or the county to receive a vaccination appointment. The state asks residents to utilize the digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn. ca.gov to determine their vaccine eligibility and schedule appointments. The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) said that appointments are prioritized for people who are most at risk for COVID-19 exposure or severe symptoms. “Vaccine distribution is being prioritized for persons who are most at risk for hospitalization or death due to COVID-19, as well as persons who are at high risk for occupational exposure,” ACPHD said on its website. “We expect to have more vaccine supply in the coming months. Eligibility criteria will continue to be updated based on capacity and vaccine availability.” People who work in Alameda County in certain sectors, like janitorial, food service, transportation and education, are also eligible for appointments. The county opened appointments to all adults a few days earlier than the state’s mandate to expand eligibility to everyone aged 16 on April 15. The county expanded eligibility to everyone aged 50 and older on April 1. Before that, vaccination was open to senior citizens, people with underlying health conditions and workers in certain industries that increase their exposure risk to COVID-19. Vaccines from Moderna and Pfizer require two doses injected several weeks apart. The Johnson & Johnson vaccine, a viral vector-type vaccine, requires only one dose, but the county stated yesterday, April 13, that it is pausing distribution of the Johnson & Johnson vaccine, following new federal recommendations. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said yesterday that “out of an abundance of caution” it recommended that health agencies suspend administering the Johnson & Johnson vaccine due to concerns about rare blood clots. To date, 6.8 million doses of Johnson & Johnson vaccine have been administered in the United States. Six cases of the rare blood clot reaction have been recorded nationwide, and one death has been reported. The six cases of blood clots all occurred in women between the ages of 18 and 48. Symptoms occurred 6 to 13 days after vaccination. Even though the blood clots appear to be exceedingly rare, people who have received the Johnson & Johnson vaccine are encouraged to monitor themselves for symptoms, like severe headache, abdominal pain, leg pain or shortness of breath within three weeks after vaccination. Anyone experiencing these symptoms should contact their health care provider immediately. Alameda County said it will cancel all existing Johnson & Johnson vaccine appointments or reschedule them for other vaccine options based on supply. “Per state and federal recommendations, Alameda County will suspend administration of the Johnson & Johnson vaccine until state and federal authorities determine it is safe to begin administering the vaccine again,” said Neetu Balram, the spokesperson for the Alameda County Public Health Department, in a statement. 4200 Piedmont residents vaccinated Over half of Piedmont’s adult population, roughly 4,200 people, have been fully vaccinated as of Monday, April 12, according to ACPHD data. The health department reports that 6,410 Piedmonters have received at least one dose, which amounts to 77 percent of the City. Piedmont is the most vaccinated municipality in the county by a large margin, but other cities are catching up. Alameda County has administered over 1 million doses of vaccine since December, and 33 percent of the county’s population is now fully vaccinated. In Oakland, almost 52 percent of the population has received at least one dose and 33 percent of Oaklanders are fully vaccinated. Even as all adult residents become eligible for vaccination, the state expects it will take several months for everyone who wants a vaccine to get one. This week, the county announced that the mass vaccination site at the Oakland Coliseum will remain open. Up to 6,000 vaccine doses are expected to be administered every day at the site. Half of the doses will be supplied by the state and the other half will be provided by Alameda and Contra Costa counties. The “megasite” also sends out mobile vaccine clinics. Overall, the county is hoping to vaccinate at least 70 to 80 percent of the population. The state has administered almost 23 million vaccine doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. The state is vaccinating an average of over 366,000 people per day, an increase compared to last week.

pages.text: Wednesday, April 14, 2021 3 COVID NEWS By Barry Eitel Alameda County opened COVID-19 vaccination appointments to all adult residents age 16 and older on Monday, April 12. Vaccines manufactured by Moderna are approved for people ages 18 and older. Pfizer vaccines are currently approved for teenagers as young as 16. Alameda County has a form to receive notifications about available appointments at covid-19. acgov.org/vaccines Californians are also encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, employer or the county to receive a vaccination appointment. The state asks residents to utilize the digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn. ca.gov to determine their vaccine eligibility and schedule appointments. The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) said that appointments are prioritized for people who are most at risk for COVID-19 exposure or severe symptoms. “Vaccine distribution is being prioritized for persons who are most at risk for hospitalization or death due to COVID-19, as well as persons who are at high risk for occupational exposure,” ACPHD said on its website. “We expect to have more vaccine supply in the coming months. Eligibility criteria will continue to be updated based on capacity and vaccine availability.” People who work in Alameda County in certain sectors, like janitorial, food service, transportation and education, are also eligible for appointments. The county opened appointments to all adults a few days earlier than the state’s mandate to expand eligibility to everyone aged 16 on April 15. The county expanded eligibility to everyone aged 50 and older on April 1. Before that, vaccination was open to senior citizens, people Vaccine appointments now open to all adults in Alameda County with underlying health conditions and workers in certain industries that increase their exposure risk to COVID-19. Vaccines from Moderna and Pfizer require two doses injected several weeks apart. The Johnson & Johnson vaccine, a viral vector-type vaccine, requires only one dose, but the county stated yesterday, April 13, that it is pausing distribution of the Johnson & Johnson vaccine, following new federal recommendations. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said yesterday that “out of an abundance of caution” it recommended that health agencies suspend administering the Johnson & Johnson vaccine due to concerns about rare blood clots. To date, 6.8 million doses of Johnson & Johnson vaccine have been administered in the United States. Six cases of the rare blood clot reaction have been recorded nationwide, and one death has been reported. The six cases of blood clots all occurred in women between the ages of 18 and 48. Symptoms occurred 6 to 13 days after vaccination. Even though the blood clots appear to be exceedingly rare, people who have received the Johnson & Johnson vaccine are encouraged to monitor themselves for symptoms, like severe headache, abdominal pain, leg pain or shortness of breath within three weeks after vaccination. Anyone experiencing these symptoms should contact their health care provider immediately. Alameda County said it will cancel all existing Johnson & Johnson vaccine appointments or reschedule them for other vaccine options based on supply. “Per state and federal recommendations, Alameda County will suspend administration of the Johnson & Johnson vaccine until state and federal authorities determine it is safe to begin administering the vaccine again,” said Neetu Balram, the spokesperson for the Alameda County Public Health Department, in a statement. 4200 Piedmont residents vaccinated Over half of Piedmont’s adult population, roughly 4,200 people, have been fully vaccinated as of Monday, April 12, according to ACPHD data. The health department reports that 6,410 Piedmonters have received at least one dose, which amounts to 77 percent of the City. Piedmont is the most vaccinated municipality in the county by a large margin, but other cities are catching up. Alameda County has administered over 1 million doses of vaccine since December, and 33 percent of the county’s population is now fully vaccinated. In Oakland, almost 52 percent of the population has received at least one dose and 33 percent of Oaklanders are fully vaccinated. Even as all adult residents become eligible for vaccination, the state expects it will take several months for everyone who wants a vaccine to get one. This week, the county announced that the mass vaccination site at the Oakland Coliseum will remain open. Up to 6,000 vaccine doses are expected to be administered every day at the site. Half of the doses will be supplied by the state and the other half will be provided by Alameda and Contra Costa counties. The “megasite” also sends out mobile vaccine clinics. Overall, the county is hoping to vaccinate at least 70 to 80 percent of the population. The state has administered almost 23 million vaccine doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. The state is vaccinating an average of over 366,000 people per day, an increase compared to last week. articles.text: The Oakland Center of the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, directed by Piedmont resident, Dr. Steve Sidney, currently has job postings for a 35-year follow-up exam of study participants who were first examined in 1985-1986. The CARDIA study, funded by the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute, is a longitudinal study of black and white men and women who were 18-30 years old at the beginning of the study and who have been followed for the development of heart disease risk factors and disease. More than 900 published scientific articles have resulted from the CARDIA study thus far. This will be the 10th examination for study participants who were initially recruited from four centers around the country, including Kaiser Permanente (KP) Health Plan members from the Berkeley-Oakland area. The examination will be conducted by the KP Northern California Division of Research at its research clinic located in the Mosswood Building, 3505 Broadway in Oakland. Positions are available for scheduling examinations, conducting exam interviews and study procedures, data management, and managing the mailing of equipment and supplies for aspects of the study conducted at the homes of participants. These positions will start in May or June of this year and end during the summer of 2022. Training will be provided. If you would like more information, please contact Dr. Sidney at steve.sidney@kp.org. articles.text: Piedmont students in grades 6-12 will receive additional time in classrooms starting April 27. All students in Piedmont and Millennium High and Piedmont Middle School will be on the same schedule (see chart). They will have 8 hours and 45 minutes per week of classroom time. After continuing pressure from parents insisting on more classroom time, the school board unanimously confirmed at a special board meeting on April 7 that Piedmont’s teachers’ union voted to approve a revised Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) adopting the expanded classroom hours. “My overwhelming feeling is relief for our secondary students,” said School Board President Cory Smegal. Piedmont Middle School students previously attended school for 2.5 hours of class per week (two periods). The increase to eight hours and forty-five minutes is still only a fraction of a normal 28-30 hour school week. The middle school will institute a “Step-In Week” schedule starting the week of April 20, in which 6th graders will attend three class periods of 1 hour, 15 minutes each, while 7th and 8th graders will attend four class periods in the week. The new schedule effectively doubles the time of instruction for high school students. Prior to the agreement, 9th graders and 10th graders were on campus one week for 8.5 hours, and 11th and 12th graders went to school on alternating weeks. Under the new schedule, cohorts will not be combined and class rosters will not change. Teachers will be responsible for processing students’ daily health screener information. This task was previously delegated to other school staff seated in front of schools prior to class. The change was made in order to get the increased number of students The new “checkerboard schedule” will be the same for all students at Piedmont and Millennium High, and the middle school. on-campus every day to their classes in a timely manner. In exchange, full-time teachers not on leave will receive a one-time $1,000 stipend. Smegal explained the financials. “On March 5, the Governor signed AB 86 COVID-19 Relief Package that includes an in-person instruction grant for schools that reopen. Piedmont qualifies for $715,145 under this grant. A portion of this grant will be used for the stipend.” “There are 205 APT members as of April 8, but they are not all full-time and a few are on leave, so the final number will be between $188,000 and $205,000,” she explained. School board meetings have been unusually long for the last 13 months, often lasting for up to five hours. They also have nearly doubled in frequency. Parent comments at meetings have consistently sent a message to open schools, increase class time, and guarantee full-time in-person class in the fall. Alissa Welch, the parent of two children, said, “It is immensely gratifying and exciting to see the middle school schedule that was developed last summer by the task force finally come to fruition.” “This expansion represents the hard work and coming-together of everyone in the community in the best interests of our secondary students. I’ve always loved this schedule for its daily touchpoints,” she added. Welch was a member of the reopening task force comprising over 100 students, parents, teachers, and administrators. To view the full text of the new agreement between teachers and PUSD, go to https://agendaonline. net/public/Meeting/Attachments/ DisplayAttachment.aspx?AttachmentID=1290213&IsArchive=0.

articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is sponsoring its second annual essay contest, open to all Piedmont high school juniors and seniors. The essay should answer the question, “Given the fragility of democracy as evidenced by the insurrection of January 6, 2021, how can your generation work to ensure that democracy in the United States is strengthened for future generations?” Contest entrants may, but are not required to, rely on outside sources that are properly cited within the text and in a bibliography. A specific format for citations or bibliography is not required, but there must be enough information to allow the judges to easily verify your sources. Citations do not count toward your total number of words. Remember that this essay is not solely a research paper and should draw on the writer’s personal experiences and insights. Essays will be judged on originality, clarity of expression, vocabulary and style, proper grammar, punctuation and spelling. Students are encouraged to have a teacher, parent or mentor review the essay prior to submission keeping in mind that all work must be the student’s own. The essay must be 250 to 500 words, excluding citations. articles.text: Alameda County teachers have been eligible for COVID-19 vaccines since February 8, when Phase 1B prioritized persons in the education field. But since vaccination history is confidential, the number of Piedmont teachers who have chosen to be vaccinated is not publicly available. California employers have the ability to require employees to get vaccinated, however they run the risk of violating the Americans with Disability Act when asking questions about medical history. In the March 24 School Board Meeting Superintendent Booker said he did not want to risk issuing even an informal survey on vaccination status to teachers. Approximately 4,200 Piedmont adults were fully vaccinated as of April 12, representing more than half of the adult population. Alameda County’s Public Health Department reports that 6,410 Piedmonters have received at least one dose, or 77% of residents, the highest in the county. Piedmont teachers are not required to be vaccinated and no clauses in the school reopening agreements stipulated that teachers would return to classes only after being vaccinated. The district applied to the county to obtain vaccination supplies and offer injections to teachers via school nurses but were not granted any. With no district-wide vaccination plan, teachers independently networked with each other to find vaccination sites and make appointments. “When appointments were first available, people got on it quickly. School nurses and Superintendent Booker were sending out emails with lots of updates,” said PHS science teacher John Savage. “We know that many teachers were offered codes for vaccinations and anecdotal reports among the community suggest that many people were vaccinated at the Oakland Coliseum and received whatever vaccine was being offered at the time,” said Piedmont school nurse Amy Goldfarb. “Much like people in the community are sharing leads, sharing strategies, and actually doing the ‘refresh, refresh, refresh’ legwork, teachers supported each other too,” said PHS science teacher Auban Willats. Piedmont parents have frequently called into the school board meetings trying to find out how many teachers have been vaccinated. Some parents feel that knowing the data is crucial to public health for not only the safety of teachers and students, but also for their family members at home.

articles.text: “He is not talking because his brother speaks for him.” “She is not talking because her sister interprets for her.” These are common comments I hear when parents are calling about their second- or third-born child, as parents wonder if this will result in the younger sibling’s language being slower to develop. Is this really a phenomenon with families who have talkative older siblings? Is there a difference in the language development of later born children? If the later born child seems language delayed, will she “grow out of it”? Parents often report that their first-born children knew and understood more words than their later born children and hypothesize that later born children do not get the same amount of attention or one-to-one interaction with a parent as the eldest child does, causing the younger sibling to speak later. The impact of birth order on language development has been studied. The research shows that while some differences emerge between first and later born children’s language development, later born children are not delayed in their language development and first-borns do not have better language skills than their siblings. Some interesting differences that emerge in the research show patterns regarding sibling language development, suggesting Siblings share more with each other than love. that perhaps the differences parents see in the early language development of their first vs second born children may be influenced by the different language environments that each child is exposed to by virtue of who is in the family and the kind of interactions they have. For example, first born children tend to reach the 50-word milestone earlier than later born children (although the later born children catch up by the 100-word milestone and there are no lasting differences in vocabulary). Perhaps this is due to the first-born’s language learning environment in which parent child interactions are often centered around direct vocabulary expansion? While first-born children show strengths in vocabulary and grammar, later-born children show strengths in conversational skills. articles.text: Piedmont will celebrate its first virtual Arbor Day on Friday, April 30. It will include youth-focused activities, a video that highlights the Heritage Tree selections this year, and a traditional tree-planting. “As a commission, we are trying to include every community member possible in this celebration, beginning with children,” said Park Commission Chair Patty Dunlap. For the first time, the celebration will include a sidewalk chalk-drawing contest for Piedmont’s younger residents. Children will be encouraged to select their favorite street tree or park tree, write the name of the tree in chalk, and then decorate the sidewalk with chalk to celebrate the tree. Parents can take a photo of the artwork and submit it to Parks Projects Manager Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmint.ca.gov. Prizes will be awarded for the most creative tree art. A 30-minute video is being created to feature footage of each designated Heritage Tree in Piedmont, including the most recent winners. Heritage Trees will be introduced by the person or the family that nominated them. KCOM technician Jason Liao assisted with the filming and production. “Jason has been all over Piedmont, capturing the beauty of not only the trees, but also the surrounding settings,” Dunlap said. Zack Parisa, a Piedmont Three Yulan Magnolia trees will be planted as part of Piedmont’s Arbor Day celebration on April 30. resident and co-founder of SilviaTerra, will be the Arbor Day guest speaker. Criticism from the World Health Organization (WHO) cast shade on European nations for “unacceptably slow vaccinations” – a stinging rebuke from a source that’s loathe to criticize any nation. Already confined to the 7 p.m. to 6 a.m. curfew, these regions, comprising nearly half the population, were already adapting to a third lockdown and dulled to the daily routine for gathering essentials – food, produce, pharma, the metro, hospitals – with little else to do. Covid- 19 is spiraling out of control and the health system is over-burdened. Intensive Care Units (ICU) in Paris are running 154% over capacity, and elsewhere in France it is 115% on average over capacity. To cope, surgery theaters are being converted to ICU units and hospitals are adding 10,000 more beds. The Saint-Denis sports stadium, with a capacity of 80,00, is being organized for injections and the government is popping out 1,700 new vaccine centers. Millions of jabs are speeding to pharmacies, nurses, and doctors. T h e g o v e r n m e n t i s phone-banking the senior population to secure vaccine appointments. By April 15, anyone age 60+ is eligible for vaccine. By early June anyone age 50+ is eligible, and by summer anyone age 18+ can be vaccinated. Any person exposed to Covid-19 who’s experiencing symptoms can ask for immediate medical attention without facing the cost or losing a paycheck for two weeks of work. An individual’s treatment cost from Covid-19 infection is not monetary, but social. The fear is about infecting other people, not going bankrupt over medical bills. France keeps people employed But through it all, more than 3.6 million French workers are on paid furlough during lockdown, according to the New York Times. By squelching a tidal wave of unemployment, the country stays ready to ramp up the economy on a day’s notice, when the data shows Covid-19 is under control. A lesson learned from the 2008 Recession for France is not taking aggressive enough steps to arrest unemployment that ballooned in 2008 to 10 percent and drove the economy into a dive bomb. It took five years to recover. In the U.S. where a $2.2 trillion relief package provides jobless benefits, the problem may prove to be that sporadic onetime checks create inadequate welfare safety nets. France disperses directly to employers, which includes reimbursement of 80% of paychecks to full-time employees. Many companies pay the remaining 20% to keep employees’ pay whole and keep people employed. Families can pay their rent and feed the children, and the economy – while not exactly zinging – is showing very little downturn in the pandemic. Most businesses are not in collapse. Furloughed employees want to get back to work and are ready tomorrow, but in America, such a sentiment appears to be a debatable issue among its electorate. Coronavirus has drained millions of families’ resources due to millions of employee layoffs and small business closures. Among European nations, the paradigm for close to full employment within the safety net is showing positive results. articles.text: Highlanders sweep Encinal, bash Castro Valley 8-2 Piedmont’s baseball team is red hot on a three-game winning streak after beating Encinal in Alameda 10-6 on Wednesday, April 7, edging past the Jets 6-5 on Friday, April 9, and bashing Castro Valley 8-2 at Humphries Diamond on Saturday, April 10. The two-game series between Piedmont and Encinal re-visited the Western Alameda County Conference’s classic rivalry in the Shoreline Division. They last played in the 2019 league championship, which the Jets won 3-1. The Highlanders won the 2018 championship against Encinal 4-2 in extra innings. Piedmont’s two wins over Encinal makes them the top team in the Shoreline Division, undefeated in six games and 9-3 overall. No league championship is planned with this year’s shortened season. Piedmont’s 6-5 victory against Encinal marked its fifth win by fewer than two runs this season, all with game-winning hits in the last two innings. “Even when we’re down, we know that we can go off at any second and bring ourselves back in the game no matter what. It brings the best out in us,” said junior infielder Nico Defazio. The game featured sophomore leadoff hitter Michael Aikawa cracking his second homer this year. He currently carries a .378 batting average with 14 hits, two HRs, 10 RBIs and 14 runs scored. Photos by Mark Aikawa Nico Defazio (8) scores the winning run against Encinal in their 6-5 win last Friday. He also hit two doubles against Castro Valley. “We were watching [their pitcher] in the bullpen and everything seemed off-speed, but he threw me a fastball and I was waiting back on it,” said Aikawa. 10-6 win vs. Encinal In last Wednesday’s game, Piedmont led 9-0 in the top of the fifth before Encinal scored its first runs. The Highlanders used three pitchers; Cal Barna got the win after four innings and nine strikeouts. Will Sprague pitched two innings, two strikeouts. Julian Scherman entered for the last inning, striking out two. Lars Derr went 2-for-5 with three RBIs and one run scored. Barna went 2-for-5 with two RBIs. Aikawa had two walks, one RBI, two runs scored. Sprague had one hit and scored two runs. 6-5 comeback win in sweep of Encinal The Comeback Kids prevailed on Friday. Trailing Encinal 5-4 going into the bottom of the sixth inning. Garren Riley got on base on a hit-by-pitch (he was plunked three times in Friday’s game). Riley stole second and Defazio drew a walk with two outs. Derr, the cleanup hitter, smacked a hard groundball through the gap between second and shortstop to score Riley and Defazio, for a 6-5 lead and his second game-winning hit of the year. Piedmont opened with four runs in the first inning, sparked Michael Aikawa with a leadoff homerun against Encinal in Friday’s 6-5 win. articles.text: Cain runs for 180 yards, scores 3 touchdowns Piedmont’s football team remained undefeated at 4-0, after defeating Washington 21-0 in Fremont on Saturday, April 10. With one game remaining in the 2021 shortened season, the Highlanders have been notified that they are the No. 1 ranked team in Division 5 (smallest enrollment) of North Coast Section. “I am so proud of the boys; two shutouts in a row. I am really proud, so proud of them,” said coach Jerome Johnson. Johnson joined Piedmont with a background as defensive coach at McClymonds, Bishop O’Dowd, and Contra Costa College. Piedmont’s record in 2019 was 3-7. In Saturday’s victory, the Highlanders’ defense got the job done with two critical takeaways in their own red zone, 80 yards allowed, and 10 tackles for loss from seven different players. “We wanted to prevent them from getting into the open field,” said hybrid safety and linebacker Joe Hempeck, who finished with seven tackles, one tackle for loss, and a critical goal-line interception. Running back Brian Cain, a senior, had another huge day, accumulating 180 yards on 21 carries for three touchdowns, one for 63 yards. In the first quarter, Washington got the opening possession and had a 4th-and-goal situation from on Piedmont’s one-yard line. The Huskies called a quarterback roll-out pass, but Cain on defense was ready. He forced a fumble which was recovered by Andy Melian. After a quick punt by PHS, the Huskies had another chance to score with a first down at Piedmont’s 9-yard line. This time, Hempeck snatched Washington’s pass near the goal line and returned it 27 yards. From its own 37-yard line, Cain shook off one defender and got by another downfield for a63- yard touchdown and a 7-0 lead. After halftime, Alex Hilton returned the kickoff to the 46-yard line, and Piedmont capped off an eight-play, five and a half minute possession with an 8-yard run by Cain for a 14-0 advantage. The Highlanders’ next score came with 6:34 left when Cain ran 2 yards for the final score, his third TD of the game. He also had a 19-yard carry during the series in which he broke three tackles. Joe Hempeck intercepted a Washington pass near his own goal line. Piedmont’s defense has posted two shutouts and allowed just seven points in three games go along with two tackles and one forced fumble. Melian had seven tackles, two sacks, and four tackles for loss. Hempeck had seven tackles, one tackle for loss, an interception, and two pass defenses. articles.text: The Annual PCA Juried Art Show returns this weekend to Piedmont Center for the Arts for its 7th year and will be open to the public starting at noon on Saturday, April 17. The show includes 35 pieces selected by guest jurors René de Guzman, Senior Curator of Art at Oakland Museum of California, and Danielle Fox, Principal of Slate Gallery in Oakland. The art was selected from more than 500 submissions. The exhibition will be open to the public for five weekends on Saturdays and Sundays, April 17 through May 16, from 12:00 noon to 2:00 p.m. each day. Thanks to a generous gift from the family of John P. Thornborrow, cash awards totaling $4,000 are allocated annually to the top award winners, with an emphasis on honoring emerging artists in the Bay Area. All visitors must register in advance. An email-based online system allows visitors to sign up for their choice of day and time slot. A health screening form listing all health protocols will be emailed to visitors with their confirmation. Register for your visit at https://bit.ly/3mwWuwT. articles.text: SF Jazz will present an online concert featuring Afro-Cuban jazz artist Dayme Arocena this Friday, April 16, at 5 p.m. The concert is part of SF Jazz’s “Fridays at Five” archival, online concert series. Arocena appears on National Public Radio’s (NPR) list of 50 favorite albums of 2015 with her album “Nueva Era.” She has been described as a cross between Celia Cruz and Aretha Franklin and has won international recognition for her unique approach to jazz. Originally from Havana, she has now become one of the most widely-recognized artists in Latin American jazz in recent years. In describing her musical influences, Arocena describes herself as an onward-looking artist with a deep understanding of where she comes from. “We don’t have this native culture [in Cuba]. We don’t have indigenous people like Maya Dayme Arocena or Quechua,” she said. “They made a country with people from everywhere. That’s what make’s Cuban culture so different.” For more information on how to watch the performance on Friday, visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ watch/.

articles.text: San Francisco Opera will stream an archival capture of Don Carlo on Saturday and Sunday, April 17-18. The production will be available for viewing through the weekend. This 2016 revival of Giuseppe Verdi’s Don Carlo utilizes the composer’s 1886 five-act version of the score. Michael Fabiano stars as Carlo, both son and heir to the king of Spain. Carlo’s love for the princess Elisabetta, played by soprano Ana Maria Martinez, is dashed when his father instead claims her as his bride. The story follows a “web of courtly intrigue and machinations,” and forces Carlo to make a fatal choice. The international, all-star cast includes German bass Rene Pape, who returns to San Francisco Opera in this production as King Philip II, Carlo’s father. Polish baritone Mariusz Kwiecien is Carlo’s friend and confidant Rodrigo, and Bulgarian mezzo-soprano Nadia Krasteva makes her company debut as Princess Eboli. The impressive set is designed by Zack Brown with lighting by Gary Marder. The opera is led by former San Francisco Opera Music Director Nicola Luisotti. The opera is sung in Italian with English subtitles available, and has a run time of approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes. This opera, and other streaming archival captures, are made available through San Francisco Opera’s “Opera is On,” an at-home digital streaming service. For more information on how to watch Don Carlo, visit https://sfopera.com/opera-is-on/ streaming/.

You can now stream George Balanchine’s full-length trilogy Jewels performed by San Francisco Ballet through April 21. The ballet told in three parts – “Emeralds,” “Rubies,” and “Diamonds” – is inspired by the ornate displays at New York City jeweler Van Cleef & Arpels. “Emeralds,” the first in the trilogy, is set to the music of Gabriel Faure. It evokes forest-green meditation in long, Romantic-era style skirts and costumes. Emeralds is influence by the French style of ballet - restrained and pristine. “Rubies” follows. and is set to music by Igor Stravinsky. Vibrant, hot hues are reminiscent of Times Square at midnight. A touch of jazz in the choreography mimics rushing crowds and pedestrians. The finale, “Diamonds,” is set to the music of Peter Tchaikovsky. It is a glittering homage to Imperial Russia, and specifically, to the style of Marius Petipa who is considered the father of classical ballet. Balanchine is also considered one of the most famous and prolific choreographers of the 20th century. Both “Rubies” and “Diamonds” are from SF Ballet’s archives. Streaming access became available last week and will be available until April 21. To obtain streaming access. visit https://www.sfballet.org/productions/digital-program-04/.

articles.text: Gold Coast Chamber Players’ season finale, “Dvorak’s America,” will conclude their collection of virtual concerts on Saturday, May 1. “Dvorak’s America” explores the impact that spirituals and Native American music had on Czech composer Antonin Dvorak during his time in America. The project, three years in the making, highlights the interconnectedness of these cultures. The program will feature the composer’s String Quintet, op. 97, and the Lento from his String Quartet op. 96, both of which are nicknamed “the American.” Original music “Within My Heart” and “Beneath the Raven Moon” by Mary Youngblood is for Native American flute. Her arrangement of “Amazing Grace” represents what Dvorak heard during his stay in America. Dvorak proclaimed that African American Spirituals are “the heart of American music,” and the genre served as perhaps the greatest Western influence on Dvorak. Spirituals that will be performed in this program include “Swing Low Sweet Chariot,” “By an’ By,” and “My Lord What a Morning.” Concluding the program will be “Goin’ Home,” from the composer’s New World Symphony. Alexander String Quartet will lead the ensemble, marking one of the first performances since their unofficial retirement and addition of their new violist, David Samuel. Violist Pamela Freund-Striplen, a frequent collaborator with the Quartet, will Gold Coast Chamber Players founder, violist Pamela FreundStriplen. join its members for Dvorak’s America. The event will be livestreamed via YouTube at 7 p.m. on Saturday, May 1. For more information and to obtain tickets, visit www.gccpmusic.com, or call (925) 283-3728.

pages.text: Wednesday, April 14, 2021 15 San Francisco Opera will present Verdi’s Don Carlo this weekend. SF Opera streaming Don Carlo April 17 and 18 By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Opera will stream an archival capture of Don Carlo on Saturday and Sunday, April 17-18. The production will be available for viewing through the weekend. This 2016 revival of Giuseppe Verdi’s Don Carlo utilizes the composer’s 1886 five-act version of the score. Michael Fabiano stars as Carlo, both son and heir to the king of Spain. Carlo’s love for the princess Elisabetta, played by soprano Ana Maria Martinez, is dashed when his father instead claims her as his bride. The story follows a “web of courtly intrigue and machinations,” and forces Carlo to make a fatal choice. The international, all-star cast includes German bass Rene Pape, who returns to San Francisco Opera in this production as King Philip II, Carlo’s father. Polish baritone Mariusz Kwiecien is Carlo’s friend and confidant Rodrigo, and Bulgarian mezzo-soprano Nadia Krasteva makes her company debut as Princess Eboli. The impressive set is designed by Zack Brown with lighting by Gary Marder. The opera is led by former San Francisco Opera Music Director Nicola Luisotti. The opera is sung in Italian with English subtitles available, and has a run time of approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes. This opera, and other streaming archival captures, are made available through San Francisco Opera’s “Opera is On,” an at-home digital streaming service. For more information on how to watch Don Carlo, visit https://sfopera.com/opera-is-on/ streaming/. SF Jazz presents Dayme Arocena concert on April 16 By Allyson Aleksey SF Jazz will present an online concert featuring Afro-Cuban jazz artist Dayme Arocena this Friday, April 16, at 5 p.m. The concert is part of SF Jazz’s “Fridays at Five” archival, online concert series. Arocena appears on National Public Radio’s (NPR) list of 50 favorite albums of 2015 with her album “Nueva Era.” She has been described as a cross between Celia Cruz and Aretha Franklin and has won international recognition for her unique approach to jazz. Originally from Havana, she has now become one of the most widely-recognized artists in Latin American jazz in recent years. That’s what make’s Cuban culture so different.” For more information on how to watch the performance on Friday, visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ watch/. articles.text: Filoli House and Gardens, located in Woodside, is hosting an exhibition entitled “Stories of Resilience” now through May 23. The exhibition puts a spotlight on individuals and identity groups who overcame injustices or were historically excluded from performing at or working at Filoli. “Stories of Resilience” highlights the continued creativety and contributions of artists, entrepreneurs, and garden professionals from a diverse background. Filoli digs into census records to tell these individuals’ stories. Visitors will learn about the ways that Japanese incarceration and the Chinese Exclusion Act affected staff and nursery employees at Filoli. The Roth family’s chef, Kee Low, emigrated from China when Chinese immigration to the U.S was suspended by the Act as a reaction to the influx of immigrants during the Gold Rush. The exhibition reveals that there were no Black staff on its premises during its time as a family home. Although Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside. the African American population in the Bay Area boomed after the end of World War II, the exhibition asserts that “the Peninsula was not a welcoming place for Black families.” The organization offers a host of digital resources that explore this assertion, all available on https://filoli.org/ exposing-racial-injustice/. They will also learn about the legacy of Bella Worn, who was a principal garden advisor and florist to the Bourn and Roth families, and who became a successful entrepreneur in 1888. By the 1920s, she had become the leading decorator of San Francisco society events and defined a “new West Coast-style of floral arrangements.” She is considered one of the first largely successful female entrepreneurs in the United States. Plan to visit Filoli to see the exhibition, or browse digital resources and blogs online at https://filoli.org/stories-of-resilience.

articles.text: Sir Henry Heyman’s graduation diploma from the Leipzig conservatory. An orchestra legitimizes a city. So does an opera house. Society has always known that. Piedmont realized this about 10 years ago when it established the Piedmont Center for the Arts which is an all-encompassing arts venue. The city also has its own chamber Orchestra. The future looks bright. Every hopeful project needs someone to initiate it. Every artistic endeavor begins this way. The community then unites, and the project is finished to the betterment of the entire community. These days, unfortunately, there is usually someone lurking in the shadows who has an ax to grind. The result is stagnation. San Francisco was fortunate to have had an organizational genius. He was the Oakland-born Sir Henry Heyman. It did not hurt that Sir Henry was one of San Francisco’s most colorful characters. He was like a musical Emperor Norton, but unlike Emperor Norton, Sir Henry was the real deal, not a fictitious character. He was born to a Jewish family in Oakland in 1855. His talent was recognized early and it was acknowledged that he was a child prodigy on the violin. The family decided to send him to Europe where he was enrolled at the illustrious Leipzig Conservatory. He graduated in 1871 with highest honors after having studied with the most famous musicians in Germany. Before returning to the U.S., he traveled the length and breadth of Europe making important and lasting friendships. In addition to being an extraordinary musician, Sir Henry was a diplomatic genius. Upon return to San Francisco, Sir Henry established the first important chamber music society. In 1881 he was selected to be the concertmaster of the newly formed San Francisco Philharmonic. He received glowing reviews in the newspapers for everything he did. Under his guidance he was helpful in organizing the musical activities of the Pan Pacific Exhibition in San Francisco in 1915. Sir Henry’s influence formed the exhibition’s orchestra. He brought in some of his world-famous friends, including Camille St. Saens and Ignacy Jan Paderewski. And this was only the beginning. The Pan Pacific exhibition’s orchestra morphed into the People’s Symphony, the forerunner of the San Francisco Symphony. Sir Henry was pals with all of the earliest conductors of the Symphony. Curiously he did not play in the orchestra. But he was certainly a driving force. Being a gregarious person, Sir Henry belonged to just about every club in San Francisco. Countless composers dedicated music to him. During the earthquake and fire of 1906, Sir Henry lost nearly everything he owned. Undeterred, he continued ever upward. He encouraged Paderewski to take roots in Paso Robles, where the Polish virtuoso pianist lived between concert tours from 1912 to 1940. In contrast, Sir Henry Heyman’s health failed him and he died in Paso Robles in 1924. The entire Bay Area mourned his passing. Sir Henry had a very good sense of humor. articles.text: On display: “Rosie Lee Tompkins: A Retrospective” Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) located on the University of California campus, has announced that it will reopen to the public following a 13-month closure due to the COVID pandemic. The museum will open on May 2 and will operate on a three-day weekly schedule thereafter. A comprehensive safety plan and protocol, developed in consultation with public health authorities, is now in place, with limited attendance, advance ticketing required, and social distancing and mask-wearing. The museum will be limited to 25% of its full capacity at any one time. Reservations are available at BAMPFA.org beginning April 21 for members, and April 22 for the general public. The museum will waive admission fees for all visitors on opening day and will offer a reduced $10 general admission fee that can be used for future admission. A free preview day will be held for BAMPFA members and UC Berkeley faculty and students. A free preview day will take place on Saturday, May 1, for essential workers. BAMPFA will reopen with the exhibition “Rosie Lee Tompkins: A Retrospective,” which opened in February 2020 and was on view for less than a month before the museum closed. The exhibition is the largest retrospective to date of the work of Tompkins, who is considered one of the most celebrated quilt makers of the twentieth century. Her work was newly re-discovered following a bequest to BAMPFA of nearly 3,000 quilts by African American artists. The exhibition has been extended through July 18 this year. In addition, three major new exhibitions will be on view: “Ulrike Ottinger / MATRIX 276,” “Beyond Boundaries: Buddhist Art of Gandhara,” and “Present Tense: Five Centuries of Colonialism in Latin American and Caribbean Art.” “As BAMPFA begins the process of safely reopening this spring, we’ll be doing so with an enormous sense of appreciation for the dedicated community of art and film lovers who have stayed connected with the museum throughout this tumultuous year,” said BAMPFA Director Julie Rodrigues Widholm. “We believe that art can provide respite during uncertain times, and in that spirit, we’re looking forward to offering our audiences a space for joy and reflection.” Visit the museum’s website (BAMPFA.org) for more re-opening information, and to reserve tickets.
articles.title: Berkeley Art Museum to reopen May 2

Saturday, April 17, 12:00 p.m. Opening of Annual Juried Art Show The 7th Annual Juried Art Show returns to the Center for an exhibition from April 17 through May 16.Gallery hours are 12:00 to 2:00 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays. From a record-high 500 submissions of original art created within the past year, 35 works of art were selected by guest jurors René de Guzman, Senior Curator of Art at Oakland Museum of California, and Danielle Fox, Principal of Slate Gallery in Oakland. Through an endowment by the family of John P. Thornborrow, cash awards of $4,000 will be awarded to the top award winners, with an emphasis on honoring emerging artists in the Bay Area. The following COVID protocols will be in place: All visitors must sign up in advance for their visit. An email-based online system will be established where visitors may sign up for their choice of day. A health screening form will be emailed to visitors with their confirmation, also listing all health requirements. The exhibition will be limited to a maximum of 20 visitors at a time. Staff will be seated at the entrance, maintaining a roster of visitors correlating to time to facilitate any needed contact tracing, performing temperature checks, and collecting health screening forms. Masks and social distancing will be observed while guests visit the exhibition and while waiting to enter, Visitors will be asked to sanitize hands on entry and to circle the exhibition in a one-way direction to prevent clustering. No food or drink will be permitted. To sign up for a time to view the show, visit: https://bit. ly/3mwWuwT. For more information, see the website: piedmontcenterforthearts.org. articles.text: It was July 16, 1942, and a defining moment for the French people. On that day, that singular day, some 13,000 French Jews were rounded up and taken to the Velodrome d’Hiver, a sports stadium, where they were kept in unspeakable conditions for days, absent water and food and sanitation. They were then transported to Beaune-la-Rolande, a transit camp, where families were separated, children from parents, wives from husbands. Their ultimate destination was Auschwitz. Most were never heard from again. What is generally not known is that the French police and the French government collaborated with the Germans in the roundup. It is an astonishing and incontrovertible fact that went unspoken for decades in France. Sarah’s Key tells the story of one family, most especially Sarah (Melusine Mayance), 10-yearsold, who, with her mother and younger brother, hear a loud knock on the door in the dark of night. Two French policemen, examining their identification papers, tell them to pack; they will be leaving immediately. On impulse, gripped by fear, Sarah takes Thomas, only fouryears-old, and locks him in their bedroom cupboard, promising to return shortly; he must not make any noise and he must remain hidden. And with the cupboard key clutched in her hand, she follows her mother and father out onto the street. They are taken to the Vel d’Hiv, as it was called. Sarah, ever mindful of the key and her promise, is frantic to return for Thomas. And so, the journey of Sarah Starzynski begins. Her story is woven together with that of Julia Jarmon (Kristin Scott Thomas), a journalist, who is writing a story in 2002 for the 60th anniversary of the Vel d’Hiv roundup. Julia begins to research the events surrounding that infamous day and soon discovers more truth than she ever contemplated. Her quest to unravel the story of Sarah grows ever more painful and disturbing, haunted by the question: how could this have happened? How could the French have been complicit in such an atrocity? Julia interviews a man who is charged with chronicling the events and he remarks to her that he is committed to putting a face to each person lost and he rejects any attempt to express what occurred in terms of numbers. And it is when he hands her a photo of Sarah and Thomas, yellow stars sewn to their coats, that she becomes profoundly moved and disturbed and committed to Sarah’s story. What makes the film ever more powerful and moving is that it is, in great part, told from the point of view of Sarah. Her journey took her into the heart of darkness, devastating and horrible, is inexplicable to those who bore witness. It would change Sarah’s life forever, as it changed Julia’s. Ultimately the key becomes a metaphor, holding the promise of opening the cupboard door. But also, Julia concludes, that key holds the promise of unlocking memories, no matter the pain inherent in their revelation. Sarah’s Key. Sarah’s Key a riveting story of A Nazi roundup of French in 1942 By Chris Honoré It was July 16, 1942, and a defining moment for the French people. On that day, that singular day, some 13,000 French Jews were rounded up and taken to the Velodrome d’Hiver, a sports stadium, where they were kept in unspeakable conditions for days, absent water and food and sanitation. They were then transported to Beaune-la-Rolande, a transit camp, where families were separated, children from parents, wives from husbands. Their ultimate destination was Auschwitz. Most were never heard from again. What is generally not known is that the French police and the French government collaborated with the Germans in the roundup. It is an astonishing and incontrovertible fact that went unspoken for decades in France. Sarah’s Key tells the story of one family, most especially Sarah (Melusine Mayance), 10-yearsold, who, with her mother and younger brother, hear a loud knock on the door in the dark of night. Two French policemen, examining their identification papers, tell them to pack; they will be leaving immediately. On impulse, gripped by fear, Sarah takes Thomas, only fouryears-old, and locks him in their bedroom cupboard, promising to return shortly; he must not make any noise and he must remain hidden. And with the cupboard key clutched in her hand, she follows her mother and father out onto the street. They are taken to the Vel d’Hiv, as it was called. Sarah, ever mindful of the key and her promise, is frantic to return for Thomas. And so, the journey of Sarah Starzynski begins. Her story is woven together with that of Julia Jarmon (Kristin Scott Thomas), a journalist, who is writing a story in 2002 for the 60th anniversary of the Vel d’Hiv roundup. Julia begins to research the events surrounding that infamous day and soon discovers more truth than she ever contemplated. Her quest to unravel the story of Sarah grows ever more painful and disturbing, haunted by the question: how could this have happened? How could the French have been complicit in such an atrocity? Julia interviews a man who is charged with chronicling the events and he remarks to her that he is committed to putting a face to each person lost and he rejects any attempt to express what occurred in terms of numbers. And it is when he hands her a photo of Sarah and Thomas, yellow stars sewn to their coats, that she becomes profoundly moved and disturbed and committed to Sarah’s story. What makes the film ever more powerful and moving is that it is, in great part, told from the point of view of Sarah. Her journey took her into the heart of darkness, devastating and horrible, is inexplicable to those who bore witness. It would change Sarah’s life forever, as it changed Julia’s. Ultimately the key becomes a metaphor, holding the promise of opening the cupboard door. But also, Julia concludes, that key holds the promise of unlocking memories, no matter the pain inherent in their revelation. Sarah’s Key. Directed by Gilles Paquet-Brenner, Starring Kristin Scott Thomas, Mélusine Mayance, Aidan Quinn and Frédéric Pierrot, 1 hr., 51 min. Rated PG-13. articles.text: “Patience is a virtue” is being taken to a whole new level in our lives, at this time as we pivot toward the next phase of the global pandemic. Readers of this column know that I am a proponent of SLOW as a hallmark of quality and beauty and soulfulness. Especially when we are talking about high-quality, handmade, consciously, and thoughtfully sourced materials. And you might guess, in my industry as an interior designer, I already navigate through the tricky territory of educating clients to calibrate their expectations. These days, because of the pandemic and its consequences, there is a new normal: even slower delivery times. Sheltering in place over this past year has created an increased demand for home services, especially interior design. And this awareness of the importance of home is not likely to leave us. Many people are not going back to work in person, even after restrictions lift. We like our homes, we like being at home, and now we want to love them, beautify them. We nourish ourselves by beautifying our spaces. What has happened globally is that the supply chain has slowed. This affects the availability and cost of raw materials as well as finished products. Even when materials are locally sourced, the international market has an impact on supply. Labor has been affected also as businesses shuttered their doors, workers fell ill, or lost family members. The human family is having this experience of loss and we are realizing how we are all interconnected. Even with somebody on the other side of the world, their loss impacts us locally. With all of the interruptions, delays, and increases in demand in our industry, we are seeing that items that used to have an 8–10- week lead time are now taking 20 weeks; 16-week lead times now are going to 24 weeks. articles.text: Organic waste includes many types of materials, but the most common one stemming from households is food waste. Organic waste in landfills accounts for 20% of methane generated in California and is also the most common material type to end up in landfills. Reducing organic waste in landfills can reduce greenhouse gas emissions, create jobs, and produce compost, all while feeding more people. California Senate Bill (SB) 1383 has plans to address all of these issues. The bill aims to reduce waste sent to landfills while getting food to people who need it. This is a win for both the environment and people. First passed in 2016 by the California Legislature, SB 1383 mandates methane reduction targets statewide. Food waste emits a lot of methane, which means that less food waste will produce less methane. This effort is especially important because methane traps far more heat than carbon dioxide and can have a larger impact on climate change. The overarching goal of SB 1383 is to help California meet its 2045 carbon neutrality goal. As residents, you may not have heard of this bill because most of the work is being done by municipalities, and residential units will not see a drastic change in service. Interestingly, this bill doesn’t target individual jurisdictions, but the state as a whole. Certain jurisdictions will have to implement many more changes than others. As a leader in waste management, Piedmont is largely compliant already, and SB 1383 should not radically change how waste is managed in the City. Nate Redinbo is Piedmont’s Civicspark and Climate fellow. He can be reached at nredibo@ piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will host a public discussion with Alameda County District Attorney Nancy O’Malley on May 6 starting at 4 p.m. She will describe the work by her department with abused and homeless women, helping them move beyond trauma into a positive future. O’Malley will address the many challenges COVID-19 has posed. She will explain the ways in which the current lack of civility in politics is impeding the pace and scale of progress for women who suffer from violence. For example, passage of the Violence Against Women Act was held up due to politics, and funding for the Victims Crime Act, which provides resources to states for victims of crime, was also reduced. O’Malley is a nationally recognized expert on issues involving violence against women, violence against persons with disabilities, and interpersonal violence including sexual assault, domestic violence, elder abuse, child abuse, stalking, and human exploitation and trafficking. She serves in the office that dates to a time when Earl Warren was the Alameda County D.A. before becoming United States Supreme Court Chief Justice. O’Malley is the first woman to serve as the County’s District Attorney. The event is free and open to all community members to register for the Zoom event, visit https:// www.lwvpiedmont.org/content. a spx?page_id= 40 02&club_ id=601389&item_id=1256825. It will be recorded and posted on the League of Women Voters of Piedmont website for those who cannot join live.

articles.text: Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had its monthly book discussion on April 5 via Zoom. Thirteen readers were on the call to discuss this month’s selection, The Splendid and the Vile, a detailed story of Winston Churchill by best-selling author Erik Larson. Participating in the discussion were Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Laura Goldman, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Albert Chen, Margie Blodgett, Bella Almanzan, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Jamie Forsythe, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. The Splendid and the Vile is Larson’s 600 plus page account of Churchill’s first year as prime minister of the United Kingdom at the start of World War II. The story begins on May 10, 1940, the day Germany invaded Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands. Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain had resigned, and King George VI appointed Churchill to replace him. The king was not enthusiastic about the choice of Churchill. Some people thought he was “flamboyant, electric, and wholly unpredictable,” as well as “capricious and meddlesome, and inclined toward dynamic action in every direction at once.” Churchill also had several personal problems. He was deeply in debt, as was his son, Randolph, who spent money freely and had lost a lot of it gambling. However, the British public came to appreciate Churchill quickly, in large part because of his powerful oratory. A prime example of this was one month later, in June 1940, in which he proclaimed, “We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills; we shall never surrender.” Larson writes that Churchill then turned to a colleague and said, under his breath, “And ... we will fight them with the butt end of broken bottles, because that’s bloody well all we’ve got.” Churchill realized that the British needed the United States’ industrial and military power to defeat Germany. Larson details Churchill’s efforts to persuade President Franklin Delano Roosevelt to help the Allies, and was overjoyed when Roosevelt signed the Lend-Lease Act into law that provided the assistance that Great Britain desperately needed. Larson focuses on Churchill and his family, but also provides a vivid account of the Blitz, the horrific German bombing of Great Britain that had the British people living in danger for many months. Larson relates Churchill’s fearless reaction to the bombings, but also the intimate experiences of a wide group of people including many ordinary Brits. Larson also profiles Churchill’s family, aides, and colleagues, providing readers with a deeper understanding of him. Larson also paints a vivid portrait of Churchill’s personality, which was intense and erratic, and, for some readers, comical. The book was generally well received by the Monday Reading group, with some exceptions. Everyone agreed that Larson and his team did a remarkable job of researching and documenting Churchill and the first year of Great Britain’s war with Germany. Readers also enjoyed Larson’s writing style. The book reads like a novel. The Splendid and the Vile has so much detail and so many personal stories that the reader not only has a full understanding of the events, but also an emotional appreciation of what life was actually like during this harrowing period for the English people. The readers found this book complementary to a previous book selection, No Ordinary Time, by American historian Doris Kearns Goodwin, which told the story of Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt during World War II. The Splendid and the Vile, however, was not everyone’s cup of tea. Some members of the group found all the information and details overwhelming. They had to struggle through it, but they did find the personal stories of Churchill’s daughter Mary, his son’s wife, Pamela, and others engaging. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, April 14, 2021 FIRST MONDAY READING GROUP First Monday Reading Group digs into Churchill Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had its monthly book discussion on April 5 via Zoom. Thirteen readers were on the call to discuss this month’s selection, The Splendid and the Vile, a detailed story of Winston Churchill by best-selling author Erik Larson. Participating in the discussion were Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Laura Goldman, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Albert Chen, Margie Blodgett, Bella Almanzan, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Jamie Forsythe, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. The Splendid and the Vile is Larson’s 600 plus page account of Churchill’s first year as prime minister of the United Kingdom at the start of World War II. The story begins on May 10, 1940, the day Germany invaded Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands. Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain had resigned, and King George VI appointed Churchill to replace him. The king was not enthusiastic about the choice of Churchill. Some people thought he was “flamboyant, electric, and wholly unpredictable,” as well as “capricious and meddlesome, and inclined toward dynamic action in every direction at once.” Churchill also had several personal problems. He was deeply in debt, as was his son, Randolph, who spent money freely and had lost a lot of it gambling. However, the British public came to appreciate Churchill quickly, in large part because of his powerful oratory. A prime example of this was one month later, in June 1940, in which he proclaimed, “We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills; we shall never surrender.” Larson writes that Churchill then turned to a colleague and said, under his breath, “And ... we will fight them with the butt end of broken bottles, because that’s bloody well all we’ve got.” Churchill realized that the British needed the United States’ industrial and military power to defeat Germany. Larson details Churchill’s efforts to persuade President Franklin Delano Roosevelt to help the Allies, and was overjoyed when Roosevelt signed the Lend-Lease Act into law that provided the assistance that Great Britain desperately needed. Larson focuses on Churchill and his family, but also provides a vivid account of the Blitz, the horrific German bombing of Great Britain that had the British people living in danger for many months. Larson relates Churchill’s fearless reaction to the bombings, but also the intimate experiences of a wide group of people including many ordinary Brits. Larson also profiles Churchill’s family, aides, and colleagues, providing readers with a deeper understanding of him. Larson also paints a vivid portrait of Churchill’s personality, which was intense and erratic, and, for some readers, comical. The book was generally well received by the Monday Reading group, with some exceptions. Everyone agreed that Larson and his team did a remarkable job of researching and documenting Churchill and the first year of Great Britain’s war with Germany. Readers also enjoyed Larson’s writing style. The book reads like a novel. The Splendid and the Vile has so much detail and so many personal stories that the reader not only has a full understanding of the events, but also an emotional appreciation of what life was actually like during this harrowing period for the English people. The readers found this book complementary to a previous book selection, No Ordinary Time, by American historian Doris Kearns Goodwin, which told the story of Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt during World War II. The Splendid and the Vile, however, was not everyone’s cup of tea. Some members of the group found all the information and details overwhelming. They had to struggle through it, but they did find the personal stories of Churchill’s daughter Mary, his son’s wife, Pamela, and others engaging. articles.text: California Coffeeberry The Piedmont Garden Club has donated $5,000 to the city to plant native California plant species as part of the Highland-Guilford Steps and Handrail project connecting the Community Hall area with Guilford Road. Former Piedmont Mayor Valerie Matzger presented the donation on behalf of the Piedmont Garden Club to the Piedmont Park Commission on April 7. “Piedmont Garden Club’s conservation focus this year has been the importance of California native plants in supporting pollinators, and other wildlife,” Matzger said. “There has been a catastrophic decline in insect and bird populations, due to several factors, among them, a loss of habitat, climate change, and pesticide use.” “If we use native plants that have evolved with these creatures, we can support our ecosystem and reverse these population declines,” she said. The plants will be grown adjacent to the project near the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. An existing path entry on Highland Avenue will be replaced by a new entry plaza. New light posts and benches will be placed along the walkway. “We used to design our gardens to be beautiful, to be just ‘eye-candy.’ Now, something much more important has come up, it impacts the natural world and us,” Matzger added. California Native Plant Week The California Native Plant Society (CNPS) has deemed April 17 through April 24 as California Native Plant Week. CNPS is a volunteer organization dedicated to the preservation and celebration of California’s native flora, founded in Berkeley in 1965. In its more than 40 year-history, the volunteer group has garnered an impressive group of volunteers, including Ansel Adams, Chief Justice Earl Warren, Linus PaulRed-flowering currant (Ribes Sanguineum) ing, Philip Munz, and Lester Rowntree. CNPS encourages Californians to explore hyperlocal gardening with native plants. Similar in scope to the Piedmont Garden Club’s plans for the Guilford project, local gardening creates “urban habitats” for local wildlife, created by native plants. Suggestions from the Piedmont Garden Club included Coffeeberry, red-flowering currant, and Manzanita. For those interested in including native foliage in their gardens, the UC Berkeley Botanical Garden has expanded its plant offerings to celebrate California Native Plant week. Plants available to purchase include California lilacs, Bush Mallows, Bush Anemone, Red Willow, and others. All can be purchased at the Garden Shop. To learn more about California Native Plant Week, and the host of gardening workshops being offered by CNPS, visit https:// www.cnps.org/california-native-plant-week. The Piedmont Highlander softball team walked into Spring Break on a high note after shutting out the Encinal Jets 12-0 in Alameda on Friday, April 9. It marks the fourth win by more than 10 runs. The team has won its last two games by a total of 32-0 after beating San Lorenzo 20-0 on April 5. Piedmont’s record improves to 6-2 overall with two games remaining. Their only losses were to Mt Eden, the defending League champion. No league playoff series or championship game is planned this year. “It’s unfortunate to have a short year with this team, but the future is bright. We have a strong program with a lot of young talent,” said coach Gene Dennard. The Highlanders led 10-0 after the top of the fourth inning with four runs in the second inning, three in the third, another three runs in the fourth, and two more in the fifth and final inning for the 12-0 shutout. Pitcher Izzy Epstein hurled a no-hitter with four strikeouts and one walk. Junior Ginger Gardner hit her first high school home run in the top of the second, and power hitter Chiarra Lundin snacked her third home run of the year in the fourth inning. Final Stats: Gardner went 2-for-4 with two RBIs and two runs scored. Lundin had her homer, two RBIs, two runs scored. Castronovo went 2-for-4, two RBIs, and a run scored. Ronen went 2-for-3, two runs, one RBI. Gerhardy had a double, one RBI and one run scored. Bell had one double, one RBI, one walk drawn. NEXT UP Piedmont (6-2) plays its final home game on Tuesday, April 20 with Hayward at 3:30 p.m. PHS then plays Alameda on Thursday, April 22 at 4:00 p.m. Ginger Gardner cracked an inside the park home run against Encinal, the first of her high school career. April 16-17 The Piedmont girls’ tennis team suffered an 8-1 loss to Campolindo in Moraga on Tuesday, April 6. “There were some close matches that could have gone either way, but it just wasn’t our best day. We committed too many double faults which put us behind the 8 ball all the time,” said coach Jim Landes. The Highlanders now look ahead to the Western Alameda County Conference Individual Singles & Doubles Tournament this weekend on Friday and Saturday, April 16-17 to be held at Alameda High School. The following week the team will play a final match with Castro Valley on Saturday, April 24. The Trojans missed nearly the entire season after being without a coaching staff. In the match with Campolindo, the Highlanders were without singles starters Makenna Thiel and Audrey Edel. The only winner on the day was Michaela Bini at No. 3 singles in a dominant victory, 6-2, 6-2. “Michaela hit a lot of strong forehands and volleys that were too much for her opponent,” explained Landes. Bridgette McEfee appeared at No. 1 singles and played to a three-set loss, 3-6, 6-3, 10-1. “Bridgette cruised in the first set, but had some double faults in the next two,” said Landes. Losses at singles include Anne Jumper at the No. 2 spot, 6-4, 6-3. Audrey Mahany battled at No. 4 singles in a 6-1, 6-3 loss. At No. 5 singles, Amanda Becker lost 6-3, 6-3, and Mara LaForte at No. 6 lost 6-4, 6-3. At No. 1 doubles, Rosie Siemers and Kate Dorman had the best match of the day in a three-set battle, ultimately losing 5-7, 6-4, 10-7. “Our top team of Kate Dorman and Rosie Siemers played well with some beautiful ground strokes and volleys. Their opponents out-served them and ended up beating us in the super breaker,” said Landes. Also at doubles was Audrey Frankel and Sofia Ferraro at No. 2, losing 6-1, 6-1. Talia Blumberg and Ava Hersch lost 6-2, 6-1 at No. 3. Audrey Edel, who played No. 1 and No.2 singles during the season, will be paired with rising star Anne Jumper as a doubled team, and Mara LaForte and Kate Dorman will make their first doubles appearance in the league championship tournament. We are recalibrating after so many years of being given to instantaneously, being promised we could have all this beauty at the click of a button. In this time, my favorite word has become Pivot! The challenges we are experiencing have made us more resilient as humans. As a designer, it is my job to help my clients through the process, to create beauty, and to manage the project, the budget, and the expectations. It is not all bad news. Sometimes I get to deliver the good news, about a solution we’ve discovered, or about items arriving on time. The over-arching good news is that we’ve reset ourselves to be more patient and resilient – as people and as a community. This moment in our culture is an opportunity to practice gratitude. To acknowledge that we who get to order new, high-quality, handmade furniture, and who get to hire a designer to help make our homes beautiful, are lucky. And when we beautify our spaces, when we nourish ourselves with beauty and quality, we feel filled up, safe, and content. We are empowered to give our gifts, be the good people we are, and contribute to those around us. We are all prone to feeling beleaguered by delays, slowness, the things we cannot control. I am feeling it too. I am excited to move on to a fresh, new chapter. I love momentum. I love to start a project, get it done, and move on. But here we all are, practicing our Buddha natures. Engaging with patience, acceptance, and gratitude. If items do come in on time, we all celebrate together. If they don’t, that’s all part of the new normal. One takeaway: Hire a designer you love, because they are going to be in your life for a good long while. When the workers are gone and you are showering in your brand-new shower for the first time, and sleeping in your new primary bedroom, you will know it will all have been worth it. And it wouldn’t have been nearly as lovely if you hadn’t hired quality professionals to help. and that all good things are truly worth the wait.
